»\\n-   [Data Persistence](persistence.html) »\\n-   `sqlite3` — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases\\n-    \\n    \\n    |\\n-   Theme Auto Light Dark |\\n\\n# [`sqlite3`](#module-sqlite3 \\\"sqlite3: A DB-API 2.0 implementation using SQLite 3.x.\\\") — DB-API 2.0 interface for SQLite databases[¶](#module-sqlite3 \\\"Link to this heading\\\")\\n\\n**Source code:** [Lib/sqlite3/](https://github.com/python/cpython/tree/3.11/Lib/sqlite3/)\\n\\nSQLite is a C library that provides a lightweight disk-based database that doesn’t require a separate server process and allows accessing the database using a nonstandard variant of the SQL query language. Some applications can use SQLite for internal data storage. It’s also possible to prototype an application using SQLite and then port the code to a larger database such as PostgreSQL or Oracle.\\n\\nThe `sqlite3` module was written by Gerhard Häring. It provides an SQL interface compliant with the DB-API 2.0 specification described by [**PEP 249**](https://peps.python.org/pep-0249/), and requires SQLite 3.7.15 or newer.\\n\\nThis document includes four main sections:\\n\\n-   [Tutorial](#sqlite3-tutorial) teaches how to use the `sqlite3` module.\\n    \\n-   [Reference](#sqlite3-reference) describes the classes and functions this module defines.\\n    \\n-   [How-to guides](#sqlite3-howtos) details how to handle specific tasks.\\n    \\n-   [Explanation](#sqlite3-explanation) provides in-depth background on transaction control.\\n    \\n\\nSee also\\n\\n[https://www.sqlite.org](https://www.sqlite.org)\\n\\nThe SQLite web page; the documentation describes the syntax and the available data types for the supported SQL dialect.\\n\\n[https://www.w3schools.com/sql/](https://www.w3schools.com/sql/)\\n\\nTutorial, reference and examples for learning SQL syntax.\\n\\n[**PEP 249**](https://peps.python.org/pep-0249/) - Database API Specification 2.0\\n\\nPEP written by Marc-André Lemburg.\\n\\n## Tutorial[¶](#tutorial \\\"Link to this heading\\\")\\n\\nIn this tutorial, you will create a database of Monty Python movies using basic `sqlite3` functionality. It assumes a fundamental understanding of database concepts, including [cursors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cursor_\\\\(databases\\\\)) and [transactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database_transaction).\\n\\nFirst, we need to create a new database and open a database connection to allow `sqlite3` to work with it. Call [`sqlite3.connect()`](#sqlite3.connect \\\"sqlite3.connect\\\") to create a connection to the database `tutorial.db` in the current working directory, implicitly creating it if it does not exist:\\n\\nimport sqlite3\\ncon \\\\= sqlite3.connect(\\\"tutorial.db\\\")\\n\\nThe returned [`Connection`](#sqlite3.Connection \\\"sqlite3.Connection\\\") object `con` represents the connection to the on-disk database.\\n\\nIn order to execute SQL statements and fetch results from SQL queries, we will need to use a database cursor. Call [`con.cursor()`](#sqlite3.Connection.cursor \\\"sqlite3.Connection.cursor\\\") to create the [`Cursor`](#sqlite3.Cursor \\\"sqlite3.Cursor\\\"):\\n\\ncur \\\\= con.cursor()\\n\\nNow that we’ve got a database connection and a cursor, we can create a database table `movie` with columns for title, release year, and review score. For simplicity, we can just use column names in the table declaration – thanks to the [flexible typing](https://www.sqlite.org/flextypegood.html) feature of SQLite, specifying the data types is optional. Execute the `CREATE TABLE` statement by calling [`cur.execute(...)`](#sqlite3.Cursor.execute \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.execute\\\"):\\n\\ncur.execute(\\\"CREATE TABLE movie(title, year, score)\\\")\\n\\nWe can verify that the new table has been created by querying the `sqlite_master` table built-in to SQLite, which should now contain an entry for the `movie` table definition (see [The Schema Table](https://www.sqlite.org/schematab.html) for details). Execute that query by calling [`cur.execute(...)`](#sqlite3.Cursor.execute \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.execute\\\"), assign the result to `res`, and call [`res.fetchone()`](#sqlite3.Cursor.fetchone \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.fetchone\\\") to fetch the resulting row:\\n\\n\\\\>>> res \\\\= cur.execute(\\\"SELECT name FROM sqlite\\\\_master\\\")\\n\\\\>>> res.fetchone()\\n('movie',)\\n\\nWe can see that the table has been created, as the query returns a [`tuple`](stdtypes.html#tuple \\\"tuple\\\") containing the table’s name. If we query `sqlite_master` for a non-existent table `spam`, `res.fetchone()` will return `None`:\\n\\n\\\\>>> res \\\\= cur.execute(\\\"SELECT name FROM sqlite\\\\_master WHERE name='spam'\\\")\\n\\\\>>> res.fetchone() is None\\nTrue\\n\\nNow, add two rows of data supplied as SQL literals by executing an `INSERT` statement, once again by calling [`cur.execute(...)`](#sqlite3.Cursor.execute \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.execute\\\"):\\n\\ncur.execute(\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    INSERT INTO movie VALUES\\n        ('Monty Python and the Holy Grail', 1975, 8.2),\\n        ('And Now for Something Completely Different', 1971, 7.5)\\n\\\"\\\"\\\")\\n\\nThe `INSERT` statement implicitly opens a transaction, which needs to be committed before changes are saved in the database (see [Transaction control](#sqlite3-controlling-transactions) for details). Call [`con.commit()`](#sqlite3.Connection.commit \\\"sqlite3.Connection.commit\\\") on the connection object to commit the transaction:\\n\\ncon.commit()\\n\\nWe can verify that the data was inserted correctly by executing a `SELECT` query. Use the now-familiar [`cur.execute(...)`](#sqlite3.Cursor.execute \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.execute\\\") to assign the result to `res`, and call [`res.fetchall()`](#sqlite3.Cursor.fetchall \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.fetchall\\\") to return all resulting rows:\\n\\n\\\\>>> res \\\\= cur.execute(\\\"SELECT score FROM movie\\\")\\n\\\\>>> res.fetchall()\\n\\\\[(8.2,), (7.5,)\\\\]\\n\\nThe result is a [`list`](stdtypes.html#list \\\"list\\\") of two `tuple`s, one per row, each containing that row’s `score` value.\\n\\nNow, insert three more rows by calling [`cur.executemany(...)`](#sqlite3.Cursor.executemany \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.executemany\\\"):\\n\\ndata \\\\= \\\\[\\n    (\\\"Monty Python Live at the Hollywood Bowl\\\", 1982, 7.9),\\n    (\\\"Monty Python's The Meaning of Life\\\", 1983, 7.5),\\n    (\\\"Monty Python's Life of Brian\\\", 1979, 8.0),\\n\\\\]\\ncur.executemany(\\\"INSERT INTO movie VALUES(?, ?, ?)\\\", data)\\ncon.commit()  \\\\# Remember to commit the transaction after executing INSERT.\\n\\nNotice that `?` placeholders are used to bind `data` to the query. Always use placeholders instead of [string formatting](../tutorial/inputoutput.html#tut-formatting) to bind Python values to SQL statements, to avoid [SQL injection attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL_injection) (see [How to use placeholders to bind values in SQL queries](#sqlite3-placeholders) for more details).\\n\\nWe can verify that the new rows were inserted by executing a `SELECT` query, this time iterating over the results of the query:\\n\\n\\\\>>> for row in cur.execute(\\\"SELECT year, title FROM movie ORDER BY year\\\"):\\n...     print(row)\\n(1971, 'And Now for Something Completely Different')\\n(1975, 'Monty Python and the Holy Grail')\\n(1979, \\\"Monty Python's Life of Brian\\\")\\n(1982, 'Monty Python Live at the Hollywood Bowl')\\n(1983, \\\"Monty Python's The Meaning of Life\\\")\\n\\nEach row is a two-item [`tuple`](stdtypes.html#tuple \\\"tuple\\\") of `(year, title)`, matching the columns selected in the query.\\n\\nFinally, verify that the database has been written to disk by calling [`con.close()`](#sqlite3.Connection.close \\\"sqlite3.Connection.close\\\") to close the existing connection, opening a new one, creating a new cursor, then querying the database:\\n\\n\\\\>>> con.close()\\n\\\\>>> new\\\\_con \\\\= sqlite3.connect(\\\"tutorial.db\\\")\\n\\\\>>> new\\\\_cur \\\\= new\\\\_con.cursor()\\n\\\\>>> res \\\\= new\\\\_cur.execute(\\\"SELECT title, year FROM movie ORDER BY score DESC\\\")\\n\\\\>>> title, year \\\\= res.fetchone()\\n\\\\>>> print(f'The highest scoring Monty Python movie is {title!r}, released in {year}')\\nThe highest scoring Monty Python movie is 'Monty Python and the Holy Grail', released in 1975\\n\\nYou’ve now created an SQLite database using the `sqlite3` module, inserted data and retrieved values from it in multiple ways.\\n\\nSee also\\n\\n-   [How-to guides](#sqlite3-howtos) for further reading:\\n    \\n    -   [How to use placeholders to bind values in SQL queries](#sqlite3-placeholders)\\n        \\n    -   [How to adapt custom Python types to SQLite values](#sqlite3-adapters)\\n        \\n    -   [How to convert SQLite values to custom Python types](#sqlite3-converters)\\n        \\n    -   [How to use the connection context manager](#sqlite3-connection-context-manager)\\n        \\n    -   [How to create and use row factories](#sqlite3-howto-row-factory)\\n        \\n-   [Explanation](#sqlite3-explanation) for in-depth background on transaction control.\\n    \\n\\n## Reference[¶](#reference \\\"Link to this heading\\\")\\n\\n### Module functions[¶](#module-functions \\\"Link to this heading\\\")\\n\\nsqlite3.connect(*database*, *timeout\\\\=5.0*, *detect\\\\_types\\\\=0*, *isolation\\\\_level\\\\='DEFERRED'*, *check\\\\_same\\\\_thread\\\\=True*, *factory\\\\=sqlite3.Connection*, *cached\\\\_statements\\\\=128*, *uri\\\\=False*)[¶](#sqlite3.connect \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nOpen a connection to an SQLite database.\\n\\nParameters:\\n\\n-   **database** ([path-like object](../glossary.html#term-path-like-object)) – The path to the database file to be opened. You can pass `\\\":memory:\\\"` to create an [SQLite database existing only in memory](https://sqlite.org/inmemorydb.html), and open a connection to it.\\n    \\n-   **timeout** ([*float*](functions.html#float \\\"float\\\")) – How many seconds the connection should wait before raising an [`OperationalError`](#sqlite3.OperationalError \\\"sqlite3.OperationalError\\\") when a table is locked. If another connection opens a transaction to modify a table, that table will be locked until the transaction is committed. Default five seconds.\\n    \\n-   **detect\\\\_types** ([*int*](functions.html#int \\\"int\\\")) – Control whether and how data types not [natively supported by SQLite](#sqlite3-types) are looked up to be converted to Python types, using the converters registered with [`register_converter()`](#sqlite3.register_converter \\\"sqlite3.register_converter\\\"). Set it to any combination (using `|`, bitwise or) of [`PARSE_DECLTYPES`](#sqlite3.PARSE_DECLTYPES \\\"sqlite3.PARSE_DECLTYPES\\\") and [`PARSE_COLNAMES`](#sqlite3.PARSE_COLNAMES \\\"sqlite3.PARSE_COLNAMES\\\") to enable this. Column names takes precedence over declared types if both flags are set. Types cannot be detected for generated fields (for example `max(data)`), even when the *detect\\\\_types* parameter is set; [`str`](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\") will be returned instead. By default (`0`), type detection is disabled.\\n    \\n-   **isolation\\\\_level** ([*str*](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\") *|* *None*) – The [`isolation_level`](#sqlite3.Connection.isolation_level \\\"sqlite3.Connection.isolation_level\\\") of the connection, controlling whether and how transactions are implicitly opened. Can be `\\\"DEFERRED\\\"` (default), `\\\"EXCLUSIVE\\\"` or `\\\"IMMEDIATE\\\"`; or `None` to disable opening transactions implicitly. See [Transaction control](#sqlite3-controlling-transactions) for more.\\n    \\n-   **check\\\\_same\\\\_thread** ([*bool*](functions.html#bool \\\"bool\\\")) – If `True` (default), [`ProgrammingError`](#sqlite3.ProgrammingError \\\"sqlite3.ProgrammingError\\\") will be raised if the database connection is used by a thread other than the one that created it. If `False`, the connection may be accessed in multiple threads; write operations may need to be serialized by the user to avoid data corruption. See [`threadsafety`](#sqlite3.threadsafety \\\"sqlite3.threadsafety\\\") for more information.\\n    \\n-   **factory** ([*Connection*](#sqlite3.Connection \\\"sqlite3.Connection\\\")) – A custom subclass of [`Connection`](#sqlite3.Connection \\\"sqlite3.Connection\\\") to create the connection with, if not the default [`Connection`](#sqlite3.Connection \\\"sqlite3.Connection\\\") class.\\n    \\n-   **cached\\\\_statements** ([*int*](functions.html#int \\\"int\\\")) – The number of statements that `sqlite3` should internally cache for this connection, to avoid parsing overhead. By default, 128 statements.\\n    \\n-   **uri** ([*bool*](functions.html#bool \\\"bool\\\")) – If set to `True`, *database* is interpreted as a URI with a file path and an optional query string. The scheme part *must* be `\\\"file:\\\"`, and the path can be relative or absolute. The query string allows passing parameters to SQLite, enabling various [How to work with SQLite URIs](#sqlite3-uri-tricks).\\n    \\n\\nReturn type:\\n\\n[*Connection*](#sqlite3.Connection \\\"sqlite3.Connection\\\")\\n\\nRaises an [auditing event](sys.html#auditing) `sqlite3.connect` with argument `database`.\\n\\nRaises an [auditing event](sys.html#auditing) `sqlite3.connect/handle` with argument `connection_handle`.\\n\\nChanged in version 3.4: Added the *uri* parameter.\\n\\nChanged in version 3.7: *database* can now also be a [path-like object](../glossary.html#term-path-like-object), not only a string.\\n\\nChanged in version 3.10: Added the `sqlite3.connect/handle` auditing event.\\n\\nsqlite3.complete\\\\_statement(*statement*)[¶](#sqlite3.complete_statement \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nReturn `True` if the string *statement* appears to contain one or more complete SQL statements. No syntactic verification or parsing of any kind is performed, other than checking that there are no unclosed string literals and the statement is terminated by a semicolon.\\n\\nFor example:\\n\\n\\\\>>> sqlite3.complete\\\\_statement(\\\"SELECT foo FROM bar;\\\")\\nTrue\\n\\\\>>> sqlite3.complete\\\\_statement(\\\"SELECT foo\\\")\\nFalse\\n\\nThis function may be useful during command-line input to determine if the entered text seems to form a complete SQL statement, or if additional input is needed before calling [`execute()`](#sqlite3.Cursor.execute \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.execute\\\").\\n\\nsqlite3.enable\\\\_callback\\\\_tracebacks(*flag*, */*)[¶](#sqlite3.enable_callback_tracebacks \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nEnable or disable callback tracebacks. By default you will not get any tracebacks in user-defined functions, aggregates, converters, authorizer callbacks etc. If you want to debug them, you can call this function with *flag* set to `True`. Afterwards, you will get tracebacks from callbacks on [`sys.stderr`](sys.html#sys.stderr \\\"sys.stderr\\\"). Use `False` to disable the feature again.\\n\\nRegister an [`unraisable hook handler`](sys.html#sys.unraisablehook \\\"sys.unraisablehook\\\") for an improved debug experience:\\n\\n\\\\>>> sqlite3.enable\\\\_callback\\\\_tracebacks(True)\\n\\\\>>> con \\\\= sqlite3.connect(\\\":memory:\\\")\\n\\\\>>> def evil\\\\_trace(stmt):\\n...     5/0\\n\\\\>>> con.set\\\\_trace\\\\_callback(evil\\\\_trace)\\n\\\\>>> def debug(unraisable):\\n...     print(f\\\"{unraisable.exc\\\\_value!r} in callback {unraisable.object.\\\\_\\\\_name\\\\_\\\\_}\\\")\\n...     print(f\\\"Error message: {unraisable.err\\\\_msg}\\\")\\n\\\\>>> import sys\\n\\\\>>> sys.unraisablehook \\\\= debug\\n\\\\>>> cur \\\\= con.execute(\\\"SELECT 1\\\")\\nZeroDivisionError('division by zero') in callback evil\\\\_trace\\nError message: None\\n\\nsqlite3.register\\\\_adapter(*type*, *adapter*, */*)[¶](#sqlite3.register_adapter \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nRegister an *adapter* [callable](../glossary.html#term-callable) to adapt the Python type *type* into an SQLite type. The adapter is called with a Python object of type *type* as its sole argument, and must return a value of a [type that SQLite natively understands](#sqlite3-types).\\n\\nsqlite3.register\\\\_converter(*typename*, *converter*, */*)[¶](#sqlite3.register_converter \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nRegister the *converter* [callable](../glossary.html#term-callable) to convert SQLite objects of type *typename* into a Python object of a specific type. The converter is invoked for all SQLite values of type *typename*; it is passed a [`bytes`](stdtypes.html#bytes \\\"bytes\\\") object and should return an object of the desired Python type. Consult the parameter *detect\\\\_types* of [`connect()`](#sqlite3.connect \\\"sqlite3.connect\\\") for information regarding how type detection works.\\n\\nNote: *typename* and the name of the type in your query are matched case-insensitively.\\n\\n### Module constants[¶](#module-constants \\\"Link to this heading\\\")\\n\\nsqlite3.PARSE\\\\_COLNAMES[¶](#sqlite3.PARSE_COLNAMES \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nPass this flag value to the *detect\\\\_types* parameter of [`connect()`](#sqlite3.connect \\\"sqlite3.connect\\\") to look up a converter function by using the type name, parsed from the query column name, as the converter dictionary key. The type name must be wrapped in square brackets (`[]`).\\n\\nSELECT p as \\\"p \\\\[point\\\\]\\\" FROM test;  ! will look up converter \\\"point\\\"\\n\\nThis flag may be combined with [`PARSE_DECLTYPES`](#sqlite3.PARSE_DECLTYPES \\\"sqlite3.PARSE_DECLTYPES\\\") using the `|` (bitwise or) operator.\\n\\nsqlite3.PARSE\\\\_DECLTYPES[¶](#sqlite3.PARSE_DECLTYPES \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nPass this flag value to the *detect\\\\_types* parameter of [`connect()`](#sqlite3.connect \\\"sqlite3.connect\\\") to look up a converter function using the declared types for each column. The types are declared when the database table is created. `sqlite3` will look up a converter function using the first word of the declared type as the converter dictionary key. For example:\\n\\nCREATE TABLE test(\\n   i integer primary key,  ! will look up a converter named \\\"integer\\\"\\n   p point,                ! will look up a converter named \\\"point\\\"\\n   n number(10)            ! will look up a converter named \\\"number\\\"\\n )\\n\\nThis flag may be combined with [`PARSE_COLNAMES`](#sqlite3.PARSE_COLNAMES \\\"sqlite3.PARSE_COLNAMES\\\") using the `|` (bitwise or) operator.\\n\\nsqlite3.SQLITE\\\\_OK[¶](#sqlite3.SQLITE_OK \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nsqlite3.SQLITE\\\\_DENY[¶](#sqlite3.SQLITE_DENY \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nsqlite3.SQLITE\\\\_IGNORE[¶](#sqlite3.SQLITE_IGNORE \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nFlags that should be returned by the *authorizer\\\\_callback* [callable](../glossary.html#term-callable) passed to [`Connection.set_authorizer()`](#sqlite3.Connection.set_authorizer \\\"sqlite3.Connection.set_authorizer\\\"), to indicate whether:\\n\\n-   Access is allowed (`SQLITE_OK`),\\n    \\n-   The SQL statement should be aborted with an error (`SQLITE_DENY`)\\n    \\n-   The column should be treated as a `NULL` value (`SQLITE_IGNORE`)\\n    \\n\\nsqlite3.apilevel[¶](#sqlite3.apilevel \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nString constant stating the supported DB-API level. Required by the DB-API. Hard-coded to `\\\"2.0\\\"`.\\n\\nsqlite3.paramstyle[¶](#sqlite3.paramstyle \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nString constant stating the type of parameter marker formatting expected by the `sqlite3` module. Required by the DB-API. Hard-coded to `\\\"qmark\\\"`.\\n\\nNote\\n\\nThe `named` DB-API parameter style is also supported.\\n\\nsqlite3.sqlite\\\\_version[¶](#sqlite3.sqlite_version \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nVersion number of the runtime SQLite library as a [`string`](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\").\\n\\nsqlite3.sqlite\\\\_version\\\\_info[¶](#sqlite3.sqlite_version_info \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nVersion number of the runtime SQLite library as a [`tuple`](stdtypes.html#tuple \\\"tuple\\\") of [`integers`](functions.html#int \\\"int\\\").\\n\\nsqlite3.threadsafety[¶](#sqlite3.threadsafety \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nInteger constant required by the DB-API 2.0, stating the level of thread safety the `sqlite3` module supports. This attribute is set based on the default [threading mode](https://sqlite.org/threadsafe.html) the underlying SQLite library is compiled with. The SQLite threading modes are:\\n\\n1.  **Single-thread**: In this mode, all mutexes are disabled and SQLite is unsafe to use in more than a single thread at once.\\n    \\n2.  **Multi-thread**: In this mode, SQLite can be safely used by multiple threads provided that no single database connection is used simultaneously in two or more threads.\\n    \\n3.  **Serialized**: In serialized mode, SQLite can be safely used by multiple threads with no restriction.\\n    \\n\\nThe mappings from SQLite threading modes to DB-API 2.0 threadsafety levels are as follows:\\n\\nSQLite threading mode\\n\\n[threadsafety](https://peps.python.org/pep-0249/#threadsafety)\\n\\n[SQLITE\\\\_THREADSAFE](https://sqlite.org/compile.html#threadsafe)\\n\\nDB-API 2.0 meaning\\n\\nsingle-thread\\n\\n0\\n\\n0\\n\\nThreads may not share the module\\n\\nmulti-thread\\n\\n1\\n\\n2\\n\\nThreads may share the module, but not connections\\n\\nserialized\\n\\n3\\n\\n1\\n\\nThreads may share the module, connections and cursors\\n\\nChanged in version 3.11: Set *threadsafety* dynamically instead of hard-coding it to `1`.\\n\\nsqlite3.version[¶](#sqlite3.version \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nVersion number of this module as a [`string`](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\"). This is not the version of the SQLite library.\\n\\nsqlite3.version\\\\_info[¶](#sqlite3.version_info \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nVersion number of this module as a [`tuple`](stdtypes.html#tuple \\\"tuple\\\") of [`integers`](functions.html#int \\\"int\\\"). This is not the version of the SQLite library.\\n\\n### Connection objects[¶](#connection-objects \\\"Link to this heading\\\")\\n\\n*class* sqlite3.Connection[¶](#sqlite3.Connection \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nEach open SQLite database is represented by a `Connection` object, which is created using [`sqlite3.connect()`](#sqlite3.connect \\\"sqlite3.connect\\\"). Their main purpose is creating [`Cursor`](#sqlite3.Cursor \\\"sqlite3.Cursor\\\") objects, and [Transaction control](#sqlite3-controlling-transactions).\\n\\nSee also\\n\\n-   [How to use connection shortcut methods](#sqlite3-connection-shortcuts)\\n    \\n-   [How to use the connection context manager](#sqlite3-connection-context-manager)\\n    \\n\\nAn SQLite database connection has the following attributes and methods:\\n\\ncursor(*factory\\\\=Cursor*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.cursor \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCreate and return a [`Cursor`](#sqlite3.Cursor \\\"sqlite3.Cursor\\\") object. The cursor method accepts a single optional parameter *factory*. If supplied, this must be a [callable](../glossary.html#term-callable) returning an instance of [`Cursor`](#sqlite3.Cursor \\\"sqlite3.Cursor\\\") or its subclasses.\\n\\nblobopen(*table*, *column*, *row*, */*, *\\\\**, *readonly\\\\=False*, *name\\\\='main'*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.blobopen \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nOpen a [`Blob`](#sqlite3.Blob \\\"sqlite3.Blob\\\") handle to an existing BLOB.\\n\\nParameters:\\n\\n-   **table** ([*str*](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\")) – The name of the table where the blob is located.\\n    \\n-   **column** ([*str*](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\")) – The name of the column where the blob is located.\\n    \\n-   **row** ([*str*](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\")) – The name of the row where the blob is located.\\n    \\n-   **readonly** ([*bool*](functions.html#bool \\\"bool\\\")) – Set to `True` if the blob should be opened without write permissions. Defaults to `False`.\\n    \\n-   **name** ([*str*](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\")) – The name of the database where the blob is located. Defaults to `\\\"main\\\"`.\\n    \\n\\nRaises:\\n\\n[**OperationalError**](#sqlite3.OperationalError \\\"sqlite3.OperationalError\\\") – When trying to open a blob in a `WITHOUT ROWID` table.\\n\\nReturn type:\\n\\n[Blob](#sqlite3.Blob \\\"sqlite3.Blob\\\")\\n\\nNote\\n\\nThe blob size cannot be changed using the [`Blob`](#sqlite3.Blob \\\"sqlite3.Blob\\\") class. Use the SQL function `zeroblob` to create a blob with a fixed size.\\n\\nNew in version 3.11.\\n\\ncommit()[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.commit \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCommit any pending transaction to the database. If there is no open transaction, this method is a no-op.\\n\\nrollback()[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.rollback \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nRoll back to the start of any pending transaction. If there is no open transaction, this method is a no-op.\\n\\nclose()[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.close \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nClose the database connection. Any pending transaction is not committed implicitly; make sure to [`commit()`](#sqlite3.Connection.commit \\\"sqlite3.Connection.commit\\\") before closing to avoid losing pending changes.\\n\\nexecute(*sql*, *parameters\\\\=()*, */*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.execute \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCreate a new [`Cursor`](#sqlite3.Cursor \\\"sqlite3.Cursor\\\") object and call [`execute()`](#sqlite3.Cursor.execute \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.execute\\\") on it with the given *sql* and *parameters*. Return the new cursor object.\\n\\nexecutemany(*sql*, *parameters*, */*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.executemany \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCreate a new [`Cursor`](#sqlite3.Cursor \\\"sqlite3.Cursor\\\") object and call [`executemany()`](#sqlite3.Cursor.executemany \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.executemany\\\") on it with the given *sql* and *parameters*. Return the new cursor object.\\n\\nexecutescript(*sql\\\\_script*, */*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.executescript \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCreate a new [`Cursor`](#sqlite3.Cursor \\\"sqlite3.Cursor\\\") object and call [`executescript()`](#sqlite3.Cursor.executescript \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.executescript\\\") on it with the given *sql\\\\_script*. Return the new cursor object.\\n\\ncreate\\\\_function(*name*, *narg*, *func*, *\\\\**, *deterministic\\\\=False*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.create_function \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCreate or remove a user-defined SQL function.\\n\\nParameters:\\n\\n-   **name** ([*str*](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\")) – The name of the SQL function.\\n    \\n-   **narg** ([*int*](functions.html#int \\\"int\\\")) – The number of arguments the SQL function can accept. If `-1`, it may take any number of arguments.\\n    \\n-   **func** ([callback](../glossary.html#term-callback) | None) – A [callable](../glossary.html#term-callable) that is called when the SQL function is invoked. The callable must return [a type natively supported by SQLite](#sqlite3-types). Set to `None` to remove an existing SQL function.\\n    \\n-   **deterministic** ([*bool*](functions.html#bool \\\"bool\\\")) – If `True`, the created SQL function is marked as [deterministic](https://sqlite.org/deterministic.html), which allows SQLite to perform additional optimizations.\\n    \\n\\nRaises:\\n\\n[**NotSupportedError**](#sqlite3.NotSupportedError \\\"sqlite3.NotSupportedError\\\") – If *deterministic* is used with SQLite versions older than 3.8.3.\\n\\nChanged in version 3.8: Added the *deterministic* parameter.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\n\\\\>>> import hashlib\\n\\\\>>> def md5sum(t):\\n...     return hashlib.md5(t).hexdigest()\\n\\\\>>> con \\\\= sqlite3.connect(\\\":memory:\\\")\\n\\\\>>> con.create\\\\_function(\\\"md5\\\", 1, md5sum)\\n\\\\>>> for row in con.execute(\\\"SELECT md5(?)\\\", (b\\\"foo\\\",)):\\n...     print(row)\\n('acbd18db4cc2f85cedef654fccc4a4d8',)\\n\\ncreate\\\\_aggregate(*name*, *n\\\\_arg*, *aggregate\\\\_class*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.create_aggregate \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCreate or remove a user-defined SQL aggregate function.\\n\\nParameters:\\n\\n-   **name** ([*str*](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\")) – The name of the SQL aggregate function.\\n    \\n-   **n\\\\_arg** ([*int*](functions.html#int \\\"int\\\")) – The number of arguments the SQL aggregate function can accept. If `-1`, it may take any number of arguments.\\n    \\n-   **aggregate\\\\_class** ([class](../glossary.html#term-class) | None) –\\n    \\n    A class must implement the following methods:\\n    \\n    -   `step()`: Add a row to the aggregate.\\n        \\n    -   `finalize()`: Return the final result of the aggregate as [a type natively supported by SQLite](#sqlite3-types).\\n        \\n    \\n    The number of arguments that the `step()` method must accept is controlled by *n\\\\_arg*.\\n    \\n    Set to `None` to remove an existing SQL aggregate function.\\n    \\n\\nExample:\\n\\nclass MySum:\\n    def \\\\_\\\\_init\\\\_\\\\_(self):\\n        self.count \\\\= 0\\n\\n    def step(self, value):\\n        self.count += value\\n\\n    def finalize(self):\\n        return self.count\\n\\ncon \\\\= sqlite3.connect(\\\":memory:\\\")\\ncon.create\\\\_aggregate(\\\"mysum\\\", 1, MySum)\\ncur \\\\= con.execute(\\\"CREATE TABLE test(i)\\\")\\ncur.execute(\\\"INSERT INTO test(i) VALUES(1)\\\")\\ncur.execute(\\\"INSERT INTO test(i) VALUES(2)\\\")\\ncur.execute(\\\"SELECT mysum(i) FROM test\\\")\\nprint(cur.fetchone()\\\\[0\\\\])\\n\\ncon.close()\\n\\ncreate\\\\_window\\\\_function(*name*, *num\\\\_params*, *aggregate\\\\_class*, */*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.create_window_function \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCreate or remove a user-defined aggregate window function.\\n\\nParameters:\\n\\n-   **name** ([*str*](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\")) – The name of the SQL aggregate window function to create or remove.\\n    \\n-   **num\\\\_params** ([*int*](functions.html#int \\\"int\\\")) – The number of arguments the SQL aggregate window function can accept. If `-1`, it may take any number of arguments.\\n    \\n-   **aggregate\\\\_class** ([class](../glossary.html#term-class) | None) –\\n    \\n    A class that must implement the following methods:\\n    \\n    -   `step()`: Add a row to the current window.\\n        \\n    -   `value()`: Return the current value of the aggregate.\\n        \\n    -   `inverse()`: Remove a row from the current window.\\n        \\n    -   `finalize()`: Return the final result of the aggregate as [a type natively supported by SQLite](#sqlite3-types).\\n        \\n    \\n    The number of arguments that the `step()` and `value()` methods must accept is controlled by *num\\\\_params*.\\n    \\n    Set to `None` to remove an existing SQL aggregate window function.\\n    \\n\\nRaises:\\n\\n[**NotSupportedError**](#sqlite3.NotSupportedError \\\"sqlite3.NotSupportedError\\\") – If used with a version of SQLite older than 3.25.0, which does not support aggregate window functions.\\n\\nNew in version 3.11.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\n\\\\# Example taken from https://www.sqlite.org/windowfunctions.html#udfwinfunc\\nclass WindowSumInt:\\n    def \\\\_\\\\_init\\\\_\\\\_(self):\\n        self.count \\\\= 0\\n\\n    def step(self, value):\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"Add a row to the current window.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n        self.count += value\\n\\n    def value(self):\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"Return the current value of the aggregate.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n        return self.count\\n\\n    def inverse(self, value):\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"Remove a row from the current window.\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n        self.count \\\\-= value\\n\\n    def finalize(self):\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"Return the final value of the aggregate.\\n\\n        Any clean-up actions should be placed here.\\n        \\\"\\\"\\\"\\n        return self.count\\n\\ncon \\\\= sqlite3.connect(\\\":memory:\\\")\\ncur \\\\= con.execute(\\\"CREATE TABLE test(x, y)\\\")\\nvalues \\\\= \\\\[\\n    (\\\"a\\\", 4),\\n    (\\\"b\\\", 5),\\n    (\\\"c\\\", 3),\\n    (\\\"d\\\", 8),\\n    (\\\"e\\\", 1),\\n\\\\]\\ncur.executemany(\\\"INSERT INTO test VALUES(?, ?)\\\", values)\\ncon.create\\\\_window\\\\_function(\\\"sumint\\\", 1, WindowSumInt)\\ncur.execute(\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    SELECT x, sumint(y) OVER (\\n        ORDER BY x ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING\\n    ) AS sum\\\\_y\\n    FROM test ORDER BY x\\n\\\"\\\"\\\")\\nprint(cur.fetchall())\\n\\ncreate\\\\_collation(*name*, *callable*, */*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.create_collation \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCreate a collation named *name* using the collating function *callable*. *callable* is passed two [`string`](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\") arguments, and it should return an [`integer`](functions.html#int \\\"int\\\"):\\n\\n-   `1` if the first is ordered higher than the second\\n    \\n-   `-1` if the first is ordered lower than the second\\n    \\n-   `0` if they are ordered equal\\n    \\n\\nThe following example shows a reverse sorting collation:\\n\\ndef collate\\\\_reverse(string1, string2):\\n    if string1 \\\\== string2:\\n        return 0\\n    elif string1 < string2:\\n        return 1\\n    else:\\n        return \\\\-1\\n\\ncon \\\\= sqlite3.connect(\\\":memory:\\\")\\ncon.create\\\\_collation(\\\"reverse\\\", collate\\\\_reverse)\\n\\ncur \\\\= con.execute(\\\"CREATE TABLE test(x)\\\")\\ncur.executemany(\\\"INSERT INTO test(x) VALUES(?)\\\", \\\\[(\\\"a\\\",), (\\\"b\\\",)\\\\])\\ncur.execute(\\\"SELECT x FROM test ORDER BY x COLLATE reverse\\\")\\nfor row in cur:\\n    print(row)\\ncon.close()\\n\\nRemove a collation function by setting *callable* to `None`.\\n\\nChanged in version 3.11: The collation name can contain any Unicode character. Earlier, only ASCII characters were allowed.\\n\\ninterrupt()[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.interrupt \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCall this method from a different thread to abort any queries that might be executing on the connection. Aborted queries will raise an [`OperationalError`](#sqlite3.OperationalError \\\"sqlite3.OperationalError\\\").\\n\\nset\\\\_authorizer(*authorizer\\\\_callback*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.set_authorizer \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nRegister [callable](../glossary.html#term-callable) *authorizer\\\\_callback* to be invoked for each attempt to access a column of a table in the database. The callback should return one of [`SQLITE_OK`](#sqlite3.SQLITE_OK \\\"sqlite3.SQLITE_OK\\\"), [`SQLITE_DENY`](#sqlite3.SQLITE_DENY \\\"sqlite3.SQLITE_DENY\\\"), or [`SQLITE_IGNORE`](#sqlite3.SQLITE_IGNORE \\\"sqlite3.SQLITE_IGNORE\\\") to signal how access to the column should be handled by the underlying SQLite library.\\n\\nThe first argument to the callback signifies what kind of operation is to be authorized. The second and third argument will be arguments or `None` depending on the first argument. The 4th argument is the name of the database (“main”, “temp”, etc.) if applicable. The 5th argument is the name of the inner-most trigger or view that is responsible for the access attempt or `None` if this access attempt is directly from input SQL code.\\n\\nPlease consult the SQLite documentation about the possible values for the first argument and the meaning of the second and third argument depending on the first one. All necessary constants are available in the `sqlite3` module.\\n\\nPassing `None` as *authorizer\\\\_callback* will disable the authorizer.\\n\\nChanged in version 3.11: Added support for disabling the authorizer using `None`.\\n\\nset\\\\_progress\\\\_handler(*progress\\\\_handler*, *n*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.set_progress_handler \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nRegister [callable](../glossary.html#term-callable) *progress\\\\_handler* to be invoked for every *n* instructions of the SQLite virtual machine. This is useful if you want to get called from SQLite during long-running operations, for example to update a GUI.\\n\\nIf you want to clear any previously installed progress handler, call the method with `None` for *progress\\\\_handler*.\\n\\nReturning a non-zero value from the handler function will terminate the currently executing query and cause it to raise an [`OperationalError`](#sqlite3.OperationalError \\\"sqlite3.OperationalError\\\") exception.\\n\\nset\\\\_trace\\\\_callback(*trace\\\\_callback*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.set_trace_callback \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nRegister [callable](../glossary.html#term-callable) *trace\\\\_callback* to be invoked for each SQL statement that is actually executed by the SQLite backend.\\n\\nThe only argument passed to the callback is the statement (as [`str`](stdtypes.html#str \\\"str\\\")) that is being executed. The return value of the callback is ignored. Note that the backend does not only run statements passed to the [`Cursor.execute()`](#sqlite3.Cursor.execute \\\"sqlite3.Cursor.execute\\\") methods. Other sources include the [transaction management](#sqlite3-controlling-transactions) of the `sqlite3` module and the execution of triggers defined in the current database.\\n\\nPassing `None` as *trace\\\\_callback* will disable the trace callback.\\n\\nNote\\n\\nExceptions raised in the trace callback are not propagated. As a development and debugging aid, use [`enable_callback_tracebacks()`](#sqlite3.enable_callback_tracebacks \\\"sqlite3.enable_callback_tracebacks\\\") to enable printing tracebacks from exceptions raised in the trace callback.\\n\\nNew in version 3.3.\\n\\nenable\\\\_load\\\\_extension(*enabled*, */*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.enable_load_extension \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nEnable the SQLite engine to load SQLite extensions from shared libraries if *enabled* is `True`; else, disallow loading SQLite extensions. SQLite extensions can define new functions, aggregates or whole new virtual table implementations. One well-known extension is the fulltext-search extension distributed with SQLite.\\n\\nNote\\n\\nThe `sqlite3` module is not built with loadable extension support by default, because some platforms (notably macOS) have SQLite libraries which are compiled without this feature. To get loadable extension support, you must pass the [`--enable-loadable-sqlite-extensions`](../using/configure.html#cmdoption-enable-loadable-sqlite-extensions) option to **configure**.\\n\\nRaises an [auditing event](sys.html#auditing) `sqlite3.enable_load_extension` with arguments `connection`, `enabled`.\\n\\nNew in version 3.2.\\n\\nChanged in version 3.10: Added the `sqlite3.enable_load_extension` auditing event.\\n\\ncon.enable\\\\_load\\\\_extension(True)\\n\\n\\\\# Load the fulltext search extension\\ncon.execute(\\\"select load\\\\_extension('./fts3.so')\\\")\\n\\n\\\\# alternatively you can load the extension using an API call:\\n\\\\# con.load\\\\_extension(\\\"./fts3.so\\\")\\n\\n\\\\# disable extension loading again\\ncon.enable\\\\_load\\\\_extension(False)\\n\\n\\\\# example from SQLite wiki\\ncon.execute(\\\"CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE recipe USING fts3(name, ingredients)\\\")\\ncon.executescript(\\\"\\\"\\\"\\n    INSERT INTO recipe (name, ingredients) VALUES('broccoli stew', 'broccoli peppers cheese tomatoes');\\n    INSERT INTO recipe (name, ingredients) VALUES('pumpkin stew', 'pumpkin onions garlic celery');\\n    INSERT INTO recipe (name, ingredients) VALUES('broccoli pie', 'broccoli cheese onions flour');\\n    INSERT INTO recipe (name, ingredients) VALUES('pumpkin pie', 'pumpkin sugar flour butter');\\n    \\\"\\\"\\\")\\nfor row in con.execute(\\\"SELECT rowid, name, ingredients FROM recipe WHERE name MATCH 'pie'\\\"):\\n    print(row)\\n\\ncon.close()\\n\\nload\\\\_extension(*path*, */*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.load_extension \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nLoad an SQLite extension from a shared library located at *path*. Enable extension loading with [`enable_load_extension()`](#sqlite3.Connection.enable_load_extension \\\"sqlite3.Connection.enable_load_extension\\\") before calling this method.\\n\\nRaises an [auditing event](sys.html#auditing) `sqlite3.load_extension` with arguments `connection`, `path`.\\n\\nNew in version 3.2.\\n\\nChanged in version 3.10: Added the `sqlite3.load_extension` auditing event.\\n\\niterdump()[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.iterdump \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nReturn an [iterator](../glossary.html#term-iterator) to dump the database as SQL source code. Useful when saving an in-memory database for later restoration. Similar to the `.dump` command in the **sqlite3** shell.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\n\\\\# Convert file example.db to SQL dump file dump.sql\\ncon \\\\= sqlite3.connect('example.db')\\nwith open('dump.sql', 'w') as f:\\n    for line in con.iterdump():\\n        f.write('%s\\\\\\\\n' % line)\\ncon.close()\\n\\nSee also\\n\\n[How to handle non-UTF-8 text encodings](#sqlite3-howto-encoding)\\n\\nbackup(*target*, *\\\\**, *pages\\\\=\\\\-1*, *progress\\\\=None*, *name\\\\='main'*, *sleep\\\\=0.250*)[¶](#sqlite3.Connection.backup \\\"Link to this definition\\\")\\n\\nCreate a backup of an SQLite database.\\n\\nWorks even if the database is being accessed by other clients or concurrently by the same connection.\\n\\nParameters:\\n\\n-   **target** ([*Connection*](#sqlite3.Connection \\\"sqlite3.Connection\\\")) – The database connection to save the backup to.\\n    \\n-   **pages** ([*int*](functions.html#int \\\"int\\\")) – The number of pages to copy at a time. If equal to or less than `0`, the entire database is copied in a single step. \"msg_08c55ed93002s1xL75Ot3DNZAo\"\n-        },\n-        {\n-          \"type\": \"text\",\n-          \"text\": \"## Recommended direction\\n\\nBuild **Stock Probs as a lightweight, local web application** that answers:\\n\\n> “Using the Yahoo Finance data available at this moment, what is the estimated probability this stock rises or falls by the target close—and what sizes of move are plausible?”\\n\\nYour confirmed requirements are:\\n- Runs in the browser **on this laptop**.\\n- Supports **user-selected stocks and ETFs**.\\n- Provides **close-to-close forecasts and an intraday mode**.\\n- Preserves historical market data and **every submitted search and analysis**.\\n- Uses SQLite for storage, with verified backups.\\n- Is developed through tested Git milestones and uploaded to the existing repository.\\n\\n**The central design decision:** each forecast must retain its inputs, timestamp, model version, and result. That makes it possible to compare yesterday’s prediction with today’s outcome without rewriting what the application originally predicted.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 1. Hardware and repository findings\\n\\nThese are the specifications visible to the application runtime:\\n\\n| Component | Verified |\\n|---|---|\\n| Architecture | ARM64 / `aarch64` |\\n| CPU | 8 cores: Cortex-A55 and Cortex-A76 |\\n| Memory | 6.5 GiB total; approximately 5.7 GiB available during inspection |\\n| Swap | None |\\n| Workspace filesystem | 10 GiB total; approximately 5.9 GiB free |\\n| OS | Debian 12 |\\n| Python | 3.11.2 |\\n| SQLite | 3.40.1, with full-text search support |\\n| Current environment | NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and yfinance installed |\\n\\nThis is sufficient for the proposed application. **Disk usage and unnecessary background work deserve more attention than computing power.**\\n\\nRepository findings:\\n- The existing calculators are prototypes using hardcoded inputs and a mock backtest.\\n- The Yahoo Finance script currently has syntax errors.\\n- `burry_env/` is tracked in Git; `.venv/` is untracked.\\n- The Git object pack is already approximately 98 MiB, largely because dependencies were committed.\\n- `origin` points to [`eddiesoz/stock_probs`](https://github.com/eddiesoz/stock_probs).\\n- Remote inspection returned no advertised branches. Publication status and write access need verification.\\n- GitHub CLI, `gh`, is unavailable on the current `PATH`.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2. What the application will show\\n\\n### Analysis dashboard\\n\\nA compact dashboard with:\\n\\n- **Company/ticker search**, displaying company name, exchange, and currency before selection.\\n- Forecast mode and historical “as of” controls.\\n- Reference price, reference timestamp, target close, and data freshness.\\n- Probability of **up, down, and unchanged**.\\n- Estimated median move and **50%, 80%, and 95% prediction intervals**.\\n- Typical gain conditional on rising, and typical loss conditional on falling.\\n- Probabilities for configurable thresholds, initially **±1%, ±3%, ±5%, and ±10%**.\\n- Historical price chart and predicted return-distribution chart.\\n- Sample size, model version, and available out-of-sample performance.\\n\\nThe probabilities describe the price **at the target close**. A probability of closing down 5% is a different calculation from touching a 5% decline during the day; the interface will name the event precisely.\\n\\n### History and comparison\\n\\nA searchable history page will support:\\n- Symbol, company name, original search text, date range, mode, and success/failure filters.\\n- Reopening the **original saved result**.\\n- Running a fresh analysis from an old query.\\n- Comparing saved predictions with realized returns.\\n- CSV and JSON export.\\n\\n### Visual design\\n\\nUse a responsive layout with clear typography, restrained color, accessible contrast, and optional dark mode. Charts will have readable numerical summaries, keyboard-accessible controls, and explicit loading, stale-data, and empty states.\\n\\nCharts will be downsampled for display, while calculations use the complete eligible data. Chart.js documents downsampling and reduced animation as effective performance measures.[1]\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 3. Forecasting approach\\n\\n### A. Close-to-close: deliver first\\n\\n**Definition:** use data through the latest completed trading session to estimate the return to the next trading session’s close.\\n\\nRecommended initial model: **volatility-adjusted historical simulation**.\\n\\n1. Retrieve up to ten years of available daily history.\\n2. Establish a consistent, split-adjusted **price-return** series, retaining dividends and other corporate actions separately.\\n3. Calculate historical returns and volatility using only information available at each historical cutoff.\\n4. Standardize historical shocks by their contemporaneous volatility.\\n5. Rescale those shocks to the current volatility estimate.\\n6. Derive direction probabilities, thresholds, conditional moves, and prediction intervals from that single distribution.\\n\\nThis is a small numerical calculation suitable for the laptop. It retains historical asymmetry and large moves while responding to changes in volatility. Filtered historical simulation is an established technique, although its performance depends on the volatility estimate and available sample.[2]\\n\\n**Important modeling expectation:** volatility adjustment primarily improves estimates of move size and tail risk. Directional probabilities may remain close to historical frequencies. Any additional trend/volume-based directional model should earn its place through out-of-sample evaluation.\\n\\nThe original subjective weighting and mock “best weights” calculation will be replaced by this data-derived approach.\\n\\n### B. Intraday: a separately evaluated model\\n\\n**Definition:** estimate the move from the newest eligible intraday observation to the upcoming regular-session close.\\n\\nRecommended first implementation:\\n- Use the latest available **completed five-minute bar** as the reproducible forecast reference.\\n- Display its timestamp and age prominently; a newer quote can appear separately.\\n- Construct historical returns from comparable intraday cutoffs to their session closes.\\n- Compare observations at equivalent exchange-local times/session types.\\n- Evaluate intraday forecasts separately from daily forecasts.\\n\\nDuring an open session, the target is that session’s close. Closed-market requests will clearly identify the next target session and the available regular-session reference price.\\n\\n**Research constraint:** yfinance’s implementation limits five-minute history to approximately **60 calendar days**. That is a small number of independent trading sessions, especially for estimating rare 5–10% moves.[3]\\n\\nTherefore:\\n- Archive retrieved intraday bars locally.\\n- Backfill available gaps when the application resumes.\\n- Display limited-sample status where appropriate.\\n- Return an explicit insufficient-data result when a calculation is unsupported.\\n- Treat observations from the same session as dependent during evaluation.\\n\\n### C. Honest historical replay\\n\\nThere will be two distinct historical views:\\n\\n| View | Meaning |\\n|---|---|\\n| Saved forecast | The actual inputs and result recorded by this application at the time |\\n| Historical reconstruction | A calculation made now using historical observations cut off at the selected date |\\n\\nYahoo can revise historical prices and adjustments. A reconstruction made today cannot establish exactly what Yahoo served yesterday unless that earlier data was saved.\\n\\nCurrent news, financial statements, and earnings information can be displayed as timestamped context. Incorporating them into a historical model requires reliable publication-time data; retrospective current metadata must not enter past forecasts.\\n\\n### D. Verification of the model\\n\\nUse chronological, walk-forward evaluation:\\n- Train using earlier observations.\\n- Predict subsequent observations.\\n- Keep a final evaluation period separate from model selection.\\n- Compare against simple historical-frequency and distribution baselines.\\n- Measure direction/threshold **Brier scores**, reliability plots, and prediction-interval coverage.\\n- Report performance by symbol, mode, sample size, and evaluation period.\\n\\nTime-ordered validation avoids training on future observations.[4] Brier scores measure overall probability quality; reliability plots are also needed to assess calibration.[5]\\n\\nA rare event that has never appeared in the sample will be presented as **“no observations among N cases,”** with uncertainty, rather than as an impossible event.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 4. Simple application architecture\\n\\n```text\\nBrowser\\n  └─ FastAPI application\\n       ├─ HTML pages + small JavaScript modules + Chart.js\\n       ├─ Search / forecast / history routes\\n       ├─ Yahoo Finance adapter\\n       ├─ Forecast and evaluation functions\\n       └─ SQLite storage and backup utilities\\n```\\n\\n| Layer | Choice |\\n|---|---|\\n| Backend | Python, FastAPI, one Uvicorn worker |\\n| Frontend | Jinja2 templates, CSS, small JavaScript modules |\\n| Charts | Locally served, pinned Chart.js |\\n| Market data | yfinance behind one application-owned adapter |\\n| Numerical work | NumPy/pandas; SciPy where needed |\\n| Trading sessions | `exchange_calendars` |\\n| Persistence | Python’s built-in `sqlite3` |\\n| Dependency management | `pyproject.toml` and a committed `uv.lock` |\\n| Checks | pytest, Ruff, mypy, targeted browser tests |\\n\\nBlocking Yahoo requests will run outside the async event loop with bounded concurrency. FastAPI explicitly supports this pattern for synchronous libraries.[6]\\n\\n### Proposed project boundaries\\n\\n```text\\nsrc/stock_probs/\\n  app.py                 # Web application\\n  cli.py                 # Serve, migrate, backup, restore, evaluate\\n  providers/yahoo.py     # Yahoo-specific behavior\\n  forecasting/           # Daily/intraday models and evaluation\\n  services.py            # Fetch → validate → forecast → save\\n  db.py                  # Connections and parameterized queries\\n  templates/\\n  static/\\nmigrations/\\ntests/\\ndocs/\\n```\\n\\nLong design material belongs in `docs/PLAN.md` and `docs/MODEL.md`. The requested root `AGENTS.md` will remain compact, containing verified commands and repository-specific pitfalls.\\n\\n### Freshness and performance\\n\\n- Fetch symbols on demand.\\n- Refresh daily data when a new session may have completed.\\n- Use bounded intraday refreshes and pause browser polling when hidden.\\n- Coalesce simultaneous requests for the same data.\\n- Apply timeouts, limited retries, and backoff for Yahoo failures.\\n- Preserve usable cached results with their original timestamps.\\n- Load calendars and market data only for requested instruments.\\n\\nProposed acceptance targets, to be measured on this laptop:\\n- Normal server memory below **500 MiB**.\\n- Cached single-symbol analysis below **1 second**.\\n- Indexed history searches below **250 ms** on a 100,000-query fixture.\\n- No continuous background CPU consumption while idle.\\n\\nNetwork-dependent latency will be measured separately.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 5. SQLite, searchable history, and backups\\n\\n### Core records\\n\\n| Record | Stored information |\\n|---|---|\\n| Instruments | Canonical symbol, company, exchange, currency, timezone |\\n| Market bars | Daily/intraday OHLCV, corporate actions, timestamps, provenance |\\n| Queries | Original input, parameters, time, status, error details |\\n| Input snapshots | Immutable, compressed, deduplicated inputs used by forecasts |\\n| Forecasts | Probabilities, intervals, reference/target times, model/configuration version |\\n| Outcomes | Observed return and scoring results linked to the original forecast |\\n\\nEvery submitted company/symbol search, analysis, historical replay, and refresh will be recorded—including failures and repeated requests. Browser autocomplete keystrokes will be treated as interface activity rather than submitted queries.\\n\\nQueries will be recorded before provider work begins. Interrupted work can then be identified after a restart.\\n\\nUse indexed filters plus SQLite full-text search for original query text and company names. Historical results will remain readable offline.\\n\\n### Database behavior\\n\\nUse:\\n- Explicit transactions and foreign keys.\\n- Short writes, with network calls outside transactions.\\n- Connections owned by the thread performing the operation.\\n- A busy timeout.\\n- Versioned SQL migrations.\\n\\n**For this installation, start with rollback-journal mode.** SQLite documents a WAL-reset corruption issue affecting versions including the installed 3.40.1 under particular concurrent conditions. Rollback journaling is suitable for this workload; WAL can be reconsidered with a verified patched SQLite runtime.[7]\\n\\n### Backups\\n\\nImplement:\\n- Automatic backup when due while the application is running.\\n- A backup before schema migrations.\\n- A manual backup command.\\n- SQLite’s online backup API.\\n- Integrity checks before a backup is marked successful.\\n- Configurable retention and disk-space checks.\\n- A restore command that operates while the application is stopped.\\n- A tested restore into a separate database.\\n\\nPython’s SQLite backup API supports consistent backups while the source database is being accessed.[8]\\n\\nThe backup destination can be an external drive. **Git revisions preserve application code; database backups preserve searches, market data, and forecasts.** Query history will have no automatic expiry.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 6. Secure implementation requirements\\n\\nFor the confirmed laptop-only deployment:\\n\\n- Bind the server to `127.0.0.1`.\\n- Validate allowed Host and Origin headers and protect state-changing requests against CSRF.\\n- Use parameterized SQL and allowlisted sort/filter fields.\\n- Validate lengths, date ranges, thresholds, and Yahoo-compatible symbols.\\n- Accept stock identifiers rather than user-supplied fetch URLs.\\n- Escape company names, query text, and provider messages in HTML.\\n- Serve scripts locally under a restrictive Content Security Policy.\\n- Keep databases, backups, secrets, logs, and Yahoo cookie caches outside public static paths.\\n- Use restrictive permissions for application data.\\n- Pin dependencies and run vulnerability checks.\\n- Restrict restore operations to the local CLI.\\n- Sanitize spreadsheet exports against formula injection.\\n\\nOrigin verification and CSRF defenses remain relevant to local browser applications.[9]\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 7. Actionable implementation and Git gates\\n\\nEach milestone follows **implement → verify → review diff → commit → push → verify remote state**.\\n\\n| Gate | Actionable deliverables | Required verification |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| **1. Foundation** | Add `AGENTS.md`, README, design documents, package structure, lockfile, `.gitignore`; archive prototypes; untrack virtual environments while preserving local installations; establish GitHub access | Reproducible ARM installation; clean imports; review tracked files and credentials |\\n| **2. Persistence** | Implement migrations, query records, immutable snapshots, history repository, backup/restore CLI | Restart persistence, failed/interrupted query recording, snapshot immutability, backup/restore round trip |\\n| **3. Yahoo integration** | Add symbol/company search, daily retrieval, metadata, exchange calendars, cache policy, error handling | Fixtures for missing data, rate limits, splits, currency units, holidays, early closes, and incomplete bars; small live smoke check |\\n| **4. Daily forecasting** | Implement baseline and volatility-adjusted distributions, thresholds, historical reconstruction, outcome scoring, walk-forward reports | Future-data exclusion, probability consistency, ordered intervals, reference-price consistency, documented evaluation |\\n| **5. Dashboard — v0.1** | Build search, analysis cards, charts, query history, original-result views, exports, backup status | Browser journey from search to saved forecast to restart and retrieval; accessibility and ARM performance checks |\\n| **6. Intraday forecasts** | Add five-minute acquisition/archive, matched-cutoff model, freshness handling, session-specific targets | Cutoff alignment, partial-bar exclusion, session-grouped evaluation, limited-sample behavior, closed-market handling |\\n| **7. Full release — v0.2** | Complete security checks, documentation, CI, resource measurements, and startup workflow; update `AGENTS.md` with verified commands | Both modes exercised end-to-end; restore drill; clean installation; source and release tag verified on GitHub |\\n\\n### Essential correctness tests\\n\\nThe highest-value tests are:\\n\\n1. Appending future prices cannot change an earlier forecast.\\n2. Updating Yahoo’s cached history cannot change a saved forecast.\\n3. Downside probabilities decrease as the loss threshold increases.\\n4. Up, down, and unchanged probabilities sum to one.\\n5. Prediction intervals are correctly ordered and use the displayed reference price.\\n6. Splits and currency changes do not become artificial crashes.\\n7. Incomplete daily/intraday bars cannot enter completed-period inputs.\\n8. Search and forecast history survives restart and backup restoration.\\n9. Provider failures are recorded and distinguishable from successful forecasts.\\n10. Input and export handling resist SQL injection, XSS, and spreadsheet formula injection.\\n\\nLive Yahoo tests will be opt-in. Deterministic tests will use controlled fixtures.\\n\\n### Proposed developer commands\\n\\nThese are commands to implement during scaffolding; they do not exist yet:\\n\\n```bash\\nuv sync --locked\\n\\nuv run stock-probs db migrate\\nuv run stock-probs serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000\\n\\nuv run ruff format --check src tests\\nuv run ruff check src tests\\nuv run mypy src/stock_probs\\nuv run pytest -q -m \\\"not live and not browser\\\"\\n\\nuv run pytest tests/test_daily_forecast.py -q\\nuv run stock-probs backup\\nuv run stock-probs restore --from /path/to/backup.sqlite3\\n```\\n\\nThe foundation gate will install/authenticate `gh` as needed and verify the existing repository. User sign-in may be required. Each milestone will inspect `git status`, `git diff`, and recent commits before staging intended files. Releases will carry explicit application/model versions and Git tags.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Research references\\n\\n1. [Chart.js performance guidance](https://www.chartjs.org/docs/latest/general/performance.html)\\n2. [Bank of England: filtered historical simulation models and their competitors](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/-/media/boe/files/working-paper/2015/filtered-historical-simulation-value-at-risk-models-and-their-competitors.pdf)\\n3. [yfinance history implementation and interval limits](https://github.com/ranaroussi/yfinance/blob/main/yfinance/scrapers/history.py)\\n4. [Time-ordered validation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit.html)\\n5. [Probability calibration and scoring](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html)\\n6. [FastAPI synchronous and asynchronous execution](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/async/)\\n7. [SQLite WAL documentation and WAL-reset issue](https://sqlite.org/wal.html#the_wal_reset_bug)\\n8. \"msg_08c5ac65e002Qcb142LWWE8BPu\"\n-        },\n-        {\n-          \"type\": \"text\",\n-          \"text\": \"**Agreed—an API between the frontend and database is a mandatory architectural requirement.** I’ll make that boundary explicit in the implementation plan.\\n\\n## Updated architecture\\n\\n```text\\nBrowser frontend\\n  │\\n  │ HTTP requests / JSON responses\\n  ▼\\nFastAPI — /api/v1/*\\n  │\\n  ▼\\nApplication services\\n  ├── Yahoo Finance adapter\\n  ├── Forecasting engine\\n  └── Database repository\\n        │\\n        ▼\\n      SQLite\\n```\\n\\nThe frontend will obtain **all application data through the API**, including forecasts, market history, previous searches, and backup status.\\n\\nFastAPI can serve both the frontend’s HTML/CSS/JavaScript and the API from one process. This keeps the application lightweight while maintaining the separation you require.\\n\\n## API responsibilities\\n\\n| Endpoint | Purpose |\\n|---|---|\\n| `POST /api/v1/searches` | Submit and record a company/symbol search |\\n| `POST /api/v1/forecasts` | Request an analysis and persist its result |\\n| `GET /api/v1/forecasts/{id}` | Retrieve an original saved forecast |\\n| `GET /api/v1/history` | Search and paginate previous queries |\\n| `GET /api/v1/instruments/{id}/prices` | Retrieve historical prices |\\n| `GET /api/v1/exports?...` | Export records selected through validated filters |\\n| `GET /api/v1/backups/status` | Display backup status |\\n\\nThe API will validate requests, call application services, and return defined response formats. Database queries and connections will belong to the backend repository layer. Database files and backups will reside outside publicly served directories.\\n\\n## Changes to the implementation gates\\n\\n- **Persistence gate:** establish the backend-only database repository.\\n- **API gate:** implement and test request validation, response contracts, pagination, and error handling before connecting the dashboard.\\n- **Frontend gate:** make dashboard components consume `/api/v1/*`.\\n- **Release gate:** verify that database files are inaccessible over HTTP and browser data requests use the API exclusively.\\n\\nThis requirement will also be recorded in `AGENTS.md` when implementation begins. **The session remains in read-only planning mode; no files have been changed.**\",\n-          \"time\": {\n-            \"start\": 1789061171262,\n-            \"end\": 1789061182859\n-          },\n-          \"metadata\": {\n-            \"openai\": {\n-              \"itemId\": \"msg_04818ff80d403ed1016aa2e833341087d1b7f170f0a3ecb368\",\n-              \"phase\": \"final_answer\"\n-            }\n-          },\n-          \"id\": \"prt_08c5b083e0010dFNK0jB1dqPk9\",\n-          \"sessionID\": \"ses_f73b976e8ffekNCE6SNIanpXFb\",\n-          \"messageID\": \"msg_08c5ac65e002Qcb142LWWE8BPu\"\n-        },\n-        {\n-          \"reason\": \"stop\",\n-          \"snapshot\": \"f01c9cefaeee24a1c90cd9b95734b67c9a5862a3\",\n-          \"type\": \"step-finish\",\n-          \"tokens\": {\n-            \"total\": 128545,\n-            \"input\": 123600,\n-            \"output\": 464,\n-            \"reasoning\": 257,\n-            \"cache\": {\n-              \"write\": 0,\n-              \"read\": 4224\n-            }\n-          },\n-          \"cost\": 0,\n-          \"id\": \"prt_08c5b3960001Hq3TuHFmkBI9zJ\",\n-          \"sessionID\": \"ses_f73b976e8ffekNCE6SNIanpXFb\",\n-          \"messageID\": \"msg_08c5ac65e002Qcb142LWWE8BPu\"\n-        }\n-      ]\n-    },\n-    {\n-      \"info\": {\n-        \"role\": \"user\",\n-        \"time\": {\n-          \"created\": 1789061526783\n-        },\n-        \"agent\": \"plan\",\n-        \"model\": {\n-          \"providerID\": \"openai\",\n-          \"modelID\": \"gpt-6-astra\",\n-          \"variant\": \"xhigh\"\n-        },\n-        \"summary\": {\n-          \"diffs\": []\n-        },\n-        \"id\": \"msg_08c6074ff0018UbGjrIPyiJ9Yg\",\n-        \"sessionID\": \"ses_f73b976e8ffekNCE6SNIanpXFb\"\n-      },\n-      \"parts\": [\n-        {\n-          \"type\": \"text\",\n-          \"text\": \"One more requirement. To get started with it, refer to the [getting started guide](/python/docs/intro).\\n\\n## Usage[​](#usage \\\"Direct link to Usage\\\")\\n\\nTo run your tests, use [Pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/) CLI.\\n\\n```\\npytest --browser webkit --headed\\n```\\n\\nIf you want to add the CLI arguments automatically without specifying them, you can use the [pytest.ini](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/reference.html#ini-options-ref) file:\\n\\n```\\n# content of pytest.ini[pytest]# Run firefox with UIaddopts = --headed --browser firefox\\n```\\n\\n## CLI arguments[​](#cli-arguments \\\"Direct link to CLI arguments\\\")\\n\\nNote that CLI arguments are only applied to the default `browser`, `context` and `page` fixtures. If you create a browser, a context or a page with the API call like [browser.new\\\\_context()](/python/docs/api/class-browser#browser-new-context), the CLI arguments are not applied.\\n\\n-   `--headed`: Run tests in headed mode (default: headless).\\n-   `--browser`: Run tests in a different browser `chromium`, `firefox`, or `webkit`. It can be specified multiple times (default: `chromium`).\\n-   `--browser-channel` [Browser channel](/python/docs/browsers) to be used.\\n-   `--slowmo` Slows down Playwright operations by the specified amount of milliseconds. Useful so that you can see what is going on (default: 0).\\n-   `--device` [Device](/python/docs/emulation) to be emulated.\\n-   `--output` Directory for artifacts produced by tests (default: `test-results`).\\n-   `--tracing` Whether to record a [trace](/python/docs/trace-viewer) for each test. `on`, `off`, or `retain-on-failure` (default: `off`).\\n-   `--video` Whether to record video for each test. `on`, `off`, or `retain-on-failure` (default: `off`).\\n-   `--screenshot` Whether to automatically capture a screenshot after each test. `on`, `off`, or `only-on-failure` (default: `off`).\\n-   `--full-page-screenshot` Whether to take a full page screenshot on failure. By default, only the viewport is captured. Requires `--screenshot` to be enabled (default: `off`).\\n\\n## Fixtures[​](#fixtures \\\"Direct link to Fixtures\\\")\\n\\nThis plugin configures Playwright-specific [fixtures for pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/latest/fixture.html). To use these fixtures, use the fixture name as an argument to the test function.\\n\\n```\\ndef test_my_app_is_working(fixture_name):    pass    # Test using fixture_name    # ...\\n```\\n\\n**Function scope**: These fixtures are created when requested in a test function and destroyed when the test ends.\\n\\n-   `context`: New [browser context](/python/docs/browser-contexts) for a test.\\n-   `page`: New [browser page](/python/docs/pages) for a test.\\n-   `new_context`: Allows creating different [browser contexts](/python/docs/browser-contexts) for a test. Useful for multi-user scenarios. Accepts the same parameters as [browser.new\\\\_context()](/python/docs/api/class-browser#browser-new-context).\\n\\n**Session scope**: These fixtures are created when requested in a test function and destroyed when all tests end.\\n\\n-   `playwright`: [Playwright](/python/docs/api/class-playwright) instance.\\n-   `browser_type`: [BrowserType](/python/docs/api/class-browsertype) instance of the current browser.\\n-   `browser`: [Browser](/python/docs/api/class-browser) instance launched by Playwright.\\n-   `browser_name`: Browser name as string.\\n-   `browser_channel`: Browser channel as string.\\n-   `is_chromium`, `is_webkit`, `is_firefox`: Booleans for the respective browser types.\\n\\n**Customizing fixture options**: For `browser` and `context` fixtures, use the following fixtures to define custom launch options.\\n\\n-   `browser_type_launch_args`: Override launch arguments for [browser\\\\_type.launch()](/python/docs/api/class-browsertype#browser-type-launch). It should return a Dict.\\n-   `browser_context_args`: Override the options for [browser.new\\\\_context()](/python/docs/api/class-browser#browser-new-context). It should return a Dict.\\n-   `connect_options`: Connect to an existing browser via WebSocket endpoint. It should return a Dict with [browser\\\\_type.connect()](/python/docs/api/class-browsertype#browser-type-connect) options.\\n\\nIts also possible to override the context options ([browser.new\\\\_context()](/python/docs/api/class-browser#browser-new-context)) for a single test by using the `browser_context_args` marker:\\n\\n```\\nimport pytest@pytest.mark.browser_context_args(timezone_id=\\\"Europe/Berlin\\\", locale=\\\"en-GB\\\")def test_browser_context_args(page):    assert page.evaluate(\\\"window.navigator.userAgent\\\") == \\\"Europe/Berlin\\\"    assert page.evaluate(\\\"window.navigator.languages\\\") == [\\\"de-DE\\\"]\\n```\\n\\n## Parallelism: Running Multiple Tests at Once[​](#parallelism-running-multiple-tests-at-once \\\"Direct link to Parallelism: Running Multiple Tests at Once\\\")\\n\\nIf your tests are running on a machine with a lot of CPUs, you can speed up the overall execution time of your test suite by using [`pytest-xdist`](https://pypi.org/project/pytest-xdist/) to run multiple tests at once:\\n\\n```\\n# install dependencypip install pytest-xdist# use the --numprocesses flagpytest --numprocesses auto\\n```\\n\\nDepending on the hardware and nature of your tests, you can set `numprocesses` to be anywhere from `2` to the number of CPUs on the machine. If set too high, you may notice unexpected behavior.\\n\\nSee [Running Tests](/python/docs/running-tests) for general information on `pytest` options.\\n\\n## Examples[​](#examples \\\"Direct link to Examples\\\")\\n\\n### Configure typings for auto-completion[​](#configure-typings-for-auto-completion \\\"Direct link to Configure typings for auto-completion\\\")\\n\\ntest\\\\_my\\\\_application.py\\n\\n```\\nfrom playwright.sync_api import Pagedef test_visit_admin_dashboard(page: Page):    page.goto(\\\"/admin\\\")    # ...\\n```\\n\\nIf you're using VSCode with Pylance, these types can be inferred by enabling the `python.testing.pytestEnabled` setting so you don't need the type annotation.\\n\\n### Using multiple contexts[​](#using-multiple-contexts \\\"Direct link to Using multiple contexts\\\")\\n\\nIn order to simulate multiple users, you can create multiple [`BrowserContext`](/python/docs/browser-contexts) instances.\\n\\ntest\\\\_my\\\\_application.py\\n\\n```\\nfrom playwright.sync_api import Page, BrowserContextfrom pytest_playwright.pytest_playwright import CreateContextCallbackdef test_foo(page: Page, new_context: CreateContextCallback) -> None:    page.goto(\\\"https://example.com\\\")    context = new_context()    page2 = context.new_page()    # page and page2 are in different contexts\\n```\\n\\n### Skip test by browser[​](#skip-test-by-browser \\\"Direct link to Skip test by browser\\\")\\n\\ntest\\\\_my\\\\_application.py\\n\\n```\\nimport pytest@pytest.mark.skip_browser(\\\"firefox\\\")def test_visit_example(page):    page.goto(\\\"https://example.com\\\")    # ...\\n```\\n\\n### Run on a specific browser[​](#run-on-a-specific-browser \\\"Direct link to Run on a specific browser\\\")\\n\\nconftest.py\\n\\n```\\nimport pytest@pytest.mark.only_browser(\\\"chromium\\\")def test_visit_example(page):    page.goto(\\\"https://example.com\\\")    # ...\\n```\\n\\n### Run with a custom browser channel like Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge[​](#run-with-a-custom-browser-channel-like-google-chrome-or-microsoft-edge \\\"Direct link to Run with a custom browser channel like Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge\\\")\\n\\n```\\npytest --browser-channel chrome\\n```\\n\\ntest\\\\_my\\\\_application.py\\n\\n```\\ndef test_example(page):    page.goto(\\\"https://example.com\\\")\\n```\\n\\n### Configure base-url[​](#configure-base-url \\\"Direct link to Configure base-url\\\")\\n\\nStart Pytest with the `base-url` argument. -> Will result in http://localhost:8080/admin\\n```\\n\\n### Ignore HTTPS errors[​](#ignore-https-errors \\\"Direct link to Ignore HTTPS errors\\\")\\n\\nconftest.py\\n\\n```\\nimport pytest@pytest.fixture(scope=\\\"session\\\")def browser_context_args(browser_context_args):    return {        **browser_context_args,        \\\"ignore_https_errors\\\": True    }\\n```\\n\\n### Use custom viewport size[​](#use-custom-viewport-size \\\"Direct link to Use custom viewport size\\\")\\n\\nconftest.py\\n\\n```\\nimport pytest@pytest.fixture(scope=\\\"session\\\")def browser_context_args(browser_context_args):    return {        **browser_context_args,        \\\"viewport\\\": {            \\\"width\\\": 1920,            \\\"height\\\": 1080,        }    }\\n```\\n\\n### Device emulation / BrowserContext option overrides[​](#device-emulation--browsercontext-option-overrides \\\"Direct link to Device emulation / BrowserContext option overrides\\\")\\n\\nconftest.py\\n\\n```\\nimport pytest@pytest.fixture(scope=\\\"session\\\")def browser_context_args(browser_context_args, playwright):    iphone_11 = playwright.devices['iPhone 11 Pro']    return {        **browser_context_args,        **iphone_11,    }\\n```\\n\\nOr via the CLI `--device=\\\"iPhone 11 Pro\\\"`\\n\\n### Connect to remote browsers[​](#connect-to-remote-browsers \\\"Direct link to Connect to remote browsers\\\")\\n\\nconftest.py\\n\\n```\\nimport pytest@pytest.fixture(scope=\\\"session\\\")def connect_options():    return {        \\\"wsEndpoint\\\": \\\"ws://localhost:8080/ws\\\"    }\\n```\\n\\n### Using with `unittest.TestCase`[​](#using-with-unittesttestcase \\\"Direct link to using-with-unittesttestcase\\\")\\n\\nSee the following example for using it with `unittest.TestCase`. This has a limitation, that only a single browser can be specified and no matrix of multiple browsers gets generated when specifying multiple.\\n\\n```\\nimport pytestimport unittestfrom playwright.sync_api import Pageclass MyTest(unittest.TestCase):    @pytest.fixture(autouse=True)    def setup(self, page: Page):        self.page = page    def test_foobar(self):        self.page.goto(\\\"https://microsoft.com\\\")        self.page.locator(\\\"#foobar\\\").click()        assert self.page.evaluate(\\\"1 + 1\\\") == 2\\n```\\n\\n## Debugging[​](#debugging \\\"Direct link to Debugging\\\")\\n\\n### Use with pdb[​](#use-with-pdb \\\"Direct link to Use with pdb\\\")\\n\\nUse the `breakpoint()` statement in your test code to pause execution and get a [pdb](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pdb.html) REPL.\\n\\n```\\ndef test_bing_is_working(page):    page.goto(\\\"https://bing.com\\\")    breakpoint()    # ...\\n```\\n\\n## Deploy to CI[​](#deploy-to-ci \\\"Direct link to Deploy to CI\\\")\\n\\nSee the [guides for CI providers](/python/docs/ci) to deploy your tests to CI/CD.\\n\\n## Async Fixtures[​](#async-fixtures \\\"Direct link to Async Fixtures\\\")\\n\\nTo use async fixtures, install [`pytest-playwright-asyncio`](https://pypi.org/project/pytest-playwright-asyncio/).\\n\\nEnsure you are using `pytest-asyncio>=0.26.0` and set [`asyncio_default_test_loop_scope = session`](https://pytest-asyncio.readthedocs.io/en/v0.26.0/how-to-guides/change_default_test_loop.html) in your configuration (`pytest.ini/pyproject.toml/setup.cfg`).\\n\\n```\\nimport pytestfrom playwright.async_api import Page@pytest.mark.asyncio(loop_scope=\\\"session\\\")async def test_foo(page: Page):    await page.goto(\\\"https://github.com\\\")    # ...\\n```\\n\\n[\\n\\nPrevious\\n\\nSetting up CI\\n\\n](/python/docs/ci-intro)[\\n\\nNext\\n\\nGetting started - Freeze candidate.\\n2. Generate the complete full-session export before commit.\\n3. Review the entire export for secrets before commit.\\n4. Commit and push the candidate/export.\\n5. Obtain the external post-push CI receipt, including URL, workflow, job conclusions, and exact `head_sha`.\\n6. Record that receipt against the tested commit; do not claim that a later receipt-only commit was tested by the CI result it documents.\\n7. Preserve the receipt in the next full-session export/checkpoint.\\n\\nThe current successful run is evidence for its named single-platform jobs only. A future milestone requires a new external receipt for the exact candidate commit. gates\\n\\n### Native toolchain matrix\\n\\nOn both native `aarch64` and native `x86_64`:\\n\\n- verify host and interpreter architecture;\\n- install the pinned Python environment;\\n- run `make check`;\\n- install pinned Node, Chromium, and Linux browser dependencies;\\n- run official MCP smoke;\\n- run desktop/mobile browser regressions;\\n- run loopback readiness and forecast smoke;\\n- record resource and timeout measurements;\\n- publish architecture-specific artifacts and CI receipts.\\n\\nOne architecture passing does not confirm dual-architecture support.\\n\\n### Cross-architecture backup portability\\n\\n`M05` must test:\\n\\n- backup created on ARM64, restored and promoted on x86-64;\\n- backup created on x86-64, restored and promoted on ARM64;\\n- schema, artifacts;\\n- staging before promotion with active data protected.\\n\\n### Trust-key lifecycle\\n\\nTest on both architectures:\\n\\n- initial key creation and permission policy;\\n- signing and verification with key IDs;\\n- key rotation while retaining verification of permitted historical backups;\\n- revoked, missing, unknown, or wrong keys fail closed;\\n- keys are not embedded in
